The creator's retries are then served by the denial cache for up to 30s, so they still cannot access the newly created dashboard/folder during the window — the exact symptom being fixed. Consider invalidating denial entries on writes or using a much shorter TTL for denials of just-created resources.

Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and renderer collide on UID 0

The new denial-cache key is built from `checkReq.UserUID`, which for different identity types can be the same string. Anonymous subjects arrive as `anonymous:0` (UID `0`) and render-service subjects as `render:0` (UID `0`), so both produce the same key `namespace.perm_0_<action>_<name>_<parent>`. If an anonymous user is denied access to a dashboard (caching a denial under UID `0`), a renderer check for the same dashboard/action/folder within the 30s TTL takes the early `return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed:false}` at line 120 and is denied even though `getRendererPermissions` grants `*` for `dashboards:read`/`folders:read`. Consequence: image/PDF rendering intermittently fails to read dashboards whenever an anonymous denial was recently cached for the same resource. The key must include the identity type (and ideally use the resolved identity, not the raw subject UID).

Denial-cache write path and cache-served denial are untested

`TestService_CacheCheck`'s "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" seeds `permDenialCache` directly, so it only exercises the read path. Nothing verifies that a real denial (line 154 of service.go) writes to `permDenialCache`, nor that a second identical `Check` is subsequently answered from the denial cache without hitting the store (e.g., asserting `store.calls` stays constant on the second call). The new write path and the intended performance benefit are therefore unprotected against regressions.

permissionCacheUsage conflates the denial cache with the permission cache

The `permissionCacheUsage` metric is incremented on a denial-cache hit (line 118) as if it were a permission-cache hit, and on a permission-cache hit that ultimately denies the request it is recorded as `"false"` (line 137). Since the metric is meant to measure the permission cache, mixing in the new denial cache makes dashboards/alerts on cache effectiveness misleading (denial hits look like permission-cache hits, and permission-cache hits that deny look like misses). Consider a distinct counter for the denial cache or only recording permission-cache outcomes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grafana branch of the rules list lost its React key

In the `rules.map(...)` render, the `origin === 'grafana'` branch previously rendered `<GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} ... />` but now renders `<GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} ... />` without a `key`. The surrounding `datasource` and default branches still pass `key={key}`. Rendering a mapped array without keys produces React reconciliation warnings and, more importantly, lets React reuse component instances between rows. Each row contains RuleActionsButtons.V2, which keeps local state (delete modal, silence drawer, clone redirect); during infinite-scroll appends or list mutations this can cause state to bleed across rows (for example a delete/silence dialog belonging to the wrong rule). Add `key={key}` to the GrafanaRuleListItem.

false_negatives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and Pause menu items never render in the alert list view because they are gated on rulerRule

The Delete item is rendered under the condition `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165), and the Pause item under `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && ...` (line 123). This PR changes the list view so that GrafanaRuleListItem -> RuleActionsButtons.V2 -> AlertRuleMenu is given only `promRule` (rulerRule is undefined; see GrafanaRuleListItem's `actions: <RuleActionsButtons promRule={rule}.../>`). With `rulerRule` undefined both guards are false, so Delete and Pause disappear from the list even when the new prom-rule abilities make `canDelete`/`canPause` true. This is a regression from the previous GrafanaGroupLoader/GrafanaRuleLoader behavior, which loaded the ruler rule and passed it down. The guard is also stale: in RuleActionsButtons.V2 `handleDelete={() => showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)}` ignores the rulerRule argument entirely, so Delete can be rendered and handled without a rulerRule. PauseMenuItem only needs the ruler rule object to perform its mutation, so if pausing must stay functional in the list it needs to fetch the ruler rule on demand rather than silently hide the item.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

`useAllRulerRuleAbilities` previously computed `const isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group);`. The refactor to take a `RulerRuleDTO | undefined` plus a `RuleGroupIdentifierV2` no longer has access to the group object, so it now hardcodes `const isFederated = false;` (line 245, with a TODO). Federated rule groups (Mimir Enterprise cross-tenant federation, identified by `source_tenants`) can only be modified through the ruler on the owning tenant and were intentionally made read-only in Grafana by feeding `isFederated` into the `immutableRule` calculation. With this change `immutableRule` is false for federated rules, so Update/Pause/Restore/Delete abilities become allowed for them and users can attempt edits that Grafana cannot correctly persist. The group's `source_tenants` needs to be threaded through to keep federated rules immutable.

Test grants delete permission but asserts Delete is absent, locking in the deletion regression

The `should render correct menu actions when More button is clicked` test grants `AlertingRuleDelete` (and true folder delete access in `setFolderAccessControl`) and then asserts the menu contains exactly 4 items (`expect(menuItems.length).toBe(4)`) - silence, copy link, duplicate, export - i.e. it explicitly expects the Delete item to be missing. This encodes the bug where Delete/Pause are hidden because the list view no longer supplies a rulerRule (see AlertRuleMenu). Because of this assertion, fixing Delete in the list will make the test fail, so it should instead assert that the Delete menu item is present when the user has the delete permission.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Early interpolation bypasses the $__range splitting guard

`runSplitQuery` now interpolates each query via `applyTemplateVariables` before passing it to `querySupportsSplitting`. That check intentionally calls `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to avoid splitting queries that use `$__range`, because each split chunk would otherwise evaluate the range variable against the wrong range. After interpolation, `$__range` is replaced by a literal duration, so `isQueryWithRangeVariable` no longer matches and these queries are split. Each chunk then uses the full-range duration instead of the chunk range, producing overlapping/duplicated results for range-based aggregations. The range-variable check must inspect the original expression, or interpolation must happen after that classification.

Shard path interpolates every target twice

`runShardSplitQuery` now calls `applyTemplateVariables` on each target, then passes the already-interpolated targets into `runSplitQuery`, which also calls `applyTemplateVariables` on its targets. The updated shard test asserts five interpolation calls, confirming this double application. This is not safe to assume idempotent: `applyTemplateVariables` receives `request.filters`, so ad-hoc filters can be appended on both passes, and variable values that themselves contain `$...` patterns can be expanded a second time, changing the LogQL sent to Loki. Interpolation should occur once at the entry point, or `runSplitQuery` needs an option to skip interpolation when its caller has already done it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request logs no longer include traceID

The previous implementation explicitly appended the tracing ID from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` to every "Plugin Request Completed" log. This diff removes that block, and the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` only adds `endpoint`, `pluginId`, optional datasource fields, and `uname` to the context attributes. Unless another layer injects traceID, plugin request completion logs lose the field needed to correlate logs with traces.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

false_positives.candidate:
FromContext silently discards context when the concrete type assertion fails

`d.l.FromContext(ctx)` returns the infrastructure `log.Logger` interface, but the wrapper asserts it to `*log.ConcreteLogger` and falls back to `d.New()` if that assertion fails. If the infrastructure logger returns a context-aware wrapper or any other implementation, the fallback returns a logger without the supplied context, silently dropping all contextual fields. Since `LoggerMiddleware` now relies on this method for plugin request fields, that failure mode would make contextual logging appear enabled while losing the data.

New contextual logger middleware is untested

The only test change in this PR is updating the metrics middleware constructor call. There is no test that verifies the newly extracted `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` actually enriches the context with `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, and `uname`, nor that `LoggerMiddleware` now emits those contextual fields via `FromContext`. A regression where context attributes are dropped or not propagated would pass CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert and can be exceeded under concurrency

CreateOrUpdateDevice performs a separate CountDevices query and then, if count < deviceLimit, does an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT/ON DUPLICATE KEY. These are two independent statements with no transaction or locking, so N concurrent requests for new device IDs all observe count == limit-1 and all insert, leaving the table with limit-1+N devices. The configured device_limit is therefore not a hard cap under bursty anonymous traffic. Enforcing the limit needs the count check and the insert to be atomic (e.g. a single conditional/transactional statement or a locking advisory lock).

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected over-limit devices are cached before the DB call and bypass the limit afterward

In tagDeviceUI the device's cache key is written with localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) *before* calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. Now that TagDevice propagates the DB error (line 147) and client.go turns ErrDeviceLimitReached into a failed Authenticate, the failure happens after the cache is already populated. The local cache (localcache.New(29*time.Minute, ...)) therefore still holds the entry, so the next request from that same device hits the cache short-circuit at line 83, tagDeviceUI returns nil, TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds. Result: a device that is over the configured limit is rejected only once per ~29-minute window and is otherwise granted anonymous access, defeating the feature. The cache key must only be set after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice, or removed when the write fails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging is now synchronous on the anonymous auth path

The previous code ran TagDevice in a detached goroutine with its own timeout so anonymous authentication did not block on the device store. It is now called synchronously with the request context inside Authenticate. For every anonymous request that misses the per-device cache this adds a database round trip to authentication: when device_limit > 0 it is at least a COUNT over anon_device plus an INSERT/UPDATE. On instances serving many distinct anonymous devices (public dashboards), this makes the login/auth path DB-bound and couples anonymous auth latency (and availability) to the anon_device table. The change should preserve the non-blocking behavior while still being able to enforce the limit (e.g. only reject after a synchronous existence/limit check that is cheap, or move the enforcement off the hot path).

New auth.anonymous device_limit option is not documented

A new config key device_limit is read from the [auth.anonymous] section (cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)), but no sample configuration (conf/defaults.ini / conf/sample.ini) or reference documentation for this option is added in this PR. Operators have no way to discover the setting, its default of 0 (unlimited), or its interaction with the 30-day device window. Add the option to the config sample and the authentication configuration docs.

No test covers the limit enforcement through the service/cache path

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only exercises AnonDBStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice directly and asserts the second insert returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. There is no test that drives TagDevice/Authenticate for an over-limit device, which is exactly where the localCache ordering bug (cache set before write) makes the limit unenforced on subsequent requests. Add a test that goes through the Anonymous/AnonDeviceService path and verifies a rejected device stays rejected, and that a device under the limit still succeeds.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Normal cleanup progress is logged at Error level, including full ID lists

The new batch-cleanup code logs every batch at error level, including the complete list of IDs and the SQL condition (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). These calls happen on every cleanup cycle and every batch, even when there is nothing to delete. With cleanup scheduled every minute and a configurable batch size that can be as large as 32767 in the tests, this can emit very large error-level log entries in normal operation and make real errors hard to spot. Use debug/info for normal progress, and avoid logging unbounded ID lists.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

This PR changes the global cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute. The cleanup loop runs every cleanup job, including temporary file cleanup, snapshot deletion, dashboard-version deletion, image cleanup, short URL cleanup, query-history cleanup, and annotation cleanup. This makes all of those jobs run 10x more often on every instance, unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and with potentially significant DB/IO load. It may also increase the frequency of the annotation cleanup that is reported to deadlock. Revert this change or make the interval configurable and justify it separately.

false_positives.candidate:
MaxCount cleanup can delete beyond the configured retention count under concurrent deletes

In the MaxCount branch, the IDs to delete are selected with LIMIT/OFFSET in one statement and deleted by ID in a separate, non-transactional statement. If annotations among the newest cfg.MaxCount rows are deleted between the SELECT and DELETE (for example by a user deleting an annotation or by another cleanup process), the OFFSET window shifts. IDs that were outside the protected set at SELECT time can then be inside the newest MaxCount rows, but the DELETE still removes them, leaving fewer than MaxCount annotations and losing data beyond the configured retention policy. The previous DELETE-with-subquery made the selection and deletion atomic for this purpose. Revalidate the offset in the DELETE or otherwise make the two steps atomic/guarded.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage metric

The asynchronous DeleteCollection goroutine times the legacy call into startLegacy but then calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Legacy latency/failures are therefore attributed to unified storage, and the legacy metric is never updated. It should call recordLegacyDuration.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete metric uses object name as kind label

Delete records a successful storage duration with d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object name where the kind label belongs. This mislabels every successful delete metric and creates unbounded cardinailty/corrupted kind grouping. It should pass options.Kind like the other metric calls.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes can be canceled by request context

All write methods start their background legacy call with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) where ctx is the original HTTP request context. The server cancels that context when the request handler returns, which can happen immediately after the method returns while the goroutine is still starting. The derived context is canceled too, so the legacy fallback write can be skipped or fail spuriously. The same pattern occurs in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a fresh background context with only the needed values.

Delete tests do not mock or wait for async legacy call

TestMode3_Delete success configures only Storage.Delete, but Mode3.Delete now asynchronously invokes Legacy.Delete. There is no legacy mock expectation, so testify's mock panics with an unexpected call if the goroutine runs. TestMode3_DeleteCollection has the same issue at line 284. More generally, none of the Mode3 unit tests wait for the background goroutine, so they can pass without exercising the legacy write path and can panic or race nondeterministically. The tests should set up the legacy mock, synchronize on the goroutine, and assert the legacy call.

Independent async writes can reorder legacy state

Each write launches an independent goroutine with no per-object sequencing. A rapid create/update/delete sequence for the same object can reach LegacyStorage out of order, e.g. a delete may complete before an earlier update and leave the object deleted in unified but still present in legacy, or an older update may overwrite a newer one in legacy. Because reads only use unified storage, this divergence goes unnoticed until fallback is needed. Legacy writes need serialization per object (queue/worker) or another ordering guarantee.

Legacy Update no longer uses the object produced by unified storage

The old implementation wrapped objInfo so LegacyStorage.Update received the exact object returned by Storage.Update. The new implementation passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update, so LegacyStorage recomputes UpdatedObject against its own copy. If that copy is stale because prior asynchronous writes have not landed, or if unified storage defaulted/mutated fields, legacy can store a different object than unified storage, defeating the fallback guarantee. Capture res from Storage.Update and pass a wrapper using that object to Legacy.Update.

Legacy write failures are no longer logged

The background legacy Create path records only a metric and does not log errObjectSt. The same is true for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Previously legacy failures were logged with object and error details. Now a failed fallback write is invisible in logs, making production diagnosis much harder.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume synchronous legacy writes

The new file and unified-storage mode 3 subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately reads /api/playlists after k8s create/update/delete and asserts the legacy API already reflects the change. Mode 3 performs those legacy writes asynchronously, so the legacy request can race ahead of the background write and make these tests flaky. The mode 3 cases need an eventually/retry check for legacy consistency or should not assert immediate legacy state.

Storage failures recorded as legacy metric

In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). No legacy call has happened, so this records the storage failure and storage duration under the legacy metric. Update has the same bug at line 129. These should call recordStorageDuration instead; otherwise storage error/latency dashboards are wrong and legacy failure counts are inflated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

After the read-lock fast path misses, the function takes the write lock and unconditionally re-reads/re-parses the manifest (readWebAssetsFromFile) and republishes the cache, without re-checking entryPointAssetsCache. On a cold start, N goroutines can all observe the cache as nil under RLock, then serialize on the write lock and each perform a full file open + JSON decode of assets-manifest.json even though the first one already populated the cache. The consequence is redundant sequential I/O and CPU per waiter (a thundering herd) right at startup. Re-check `if entryPointAssetsCache != nil` (for non-dev env) immediately after acquiring the write lock to avoid this.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Write lock is held during blocking I/O

The exclusive lock (taken at line 48 and held via defer until return) covers the entire manifest read, including readWebAssetsFromFile (file open + JSON decode) and, when the CDN path is enabled, readWebAssetsFromCDN (an HTTP GET with the request context). While the writer holds the lock, all other GetWebAssets callers block on RLock, so slow disk or a slow/hanging CDN response stalls every concurrent request. In dev mode this happens on every call. A better structure is to build the result outside the lock and only hold the write lock briefly to publish it, or use sync.Once for the non-dev path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL expression feature flag is ignored; helper always returns false

In `enableSqlExpressions`, `enabled` is assigned `!h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)`, but both the `if` branch and the fall-through return `false`. The function therefore always returns false regardless of `featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions`. As a result `ReadQuery` rejects every SQL expression with `sqlExpressions is not implemented`, and enabling the documented `sqlExpressions` feature flag has no effect. If hard-disabling is intended, remove the flag check and update the flag documentation; otherwise return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stub DB makes TablesList/NewSQLCommand fail with misleading invalid-SQL error

All methods on the new in-memory DB return `not implemented`, but `pkg/expr/sql/parser.go` still calls `RunCommands` from `TablesList`. Thus `TablesList` can never parse any SQL and `NewSQLCommand` always returns `sql-invalid-sql` with the public message `error reading SQL command` for any non-empty SQL expression. That also affects the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path, which is not guarded by the new reader check, and produces a misleading 400 rather than a clear feature-disabled error. Either remove the SQL command/parser code path entirely or make the disabled state explicit at command construction.

false_positives.candidate:
No test covers disabled SQL expressions even when the feature flag is enabled

The security fix relies on the new `enableSqlExpressions` gate, but no test is added to assert that a `QueryTypeSQL` query is rejected and that the feature flag cannot re-enable it. A test with `FlagSqlExpressions` enabled would have caught the helper's always-false behavior and will help prevent a future regression that reopens the RCE/LFI path.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the full BuildIndex lock leaves same-key builds unprotected

BuildIndex now only takes cacheMu around the final map write. getOrCreateIndex still performs an unsynchronized check-then-build, so two concurrent searches or watch events for the same NamespacedResource can both enter BuildIndex. For file-backed indexes both calls can try to create/open the same Bleve directory, and for all indexes the later cache write can overwrite an index that has already received events, leaving the cache pointing at a stale snapshot. A per-key singleflight or build lock is needed, not just locking the map write.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache without the cache lock

bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu. The new log call `s.log.Info(..., s.search.TotalDocs())` in searchSupport.init runs immediately after the watch goroutine is started, and that goroutine can call getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex and write b.cache[key] under cacheMu. Concurrent map iteration and map write can panic or race. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock, or the cache access should be restructured.

false_positives.candidate:
Constructor leaks startup resources when Init fails

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) before returning, but on failure it returns nil without calling s.cancel() or s.lifecycle.Stop(). By that point searchSupport.init may already have started its background watcher, and lifecycle.Init may have acquired database or other resources. Since the caller receives nil, it cannot call Stop, so those resources and goroutines leak. The constructor should clean up/cancel on initialization failure.

Postgres storage-server startup coverage is skipped

The integration test now skips Postgres entirely. This is the test that exercises storage-server startup, which is exactly the behavior changed by moving unified-storage initialization into NewResourceServer. Without a replacement test, a Postgres startup regression, including failure of the eager index build, will not be caught. The test or environment should be fixed instead of skipping the backend.

Search event watcher panics on closed event channel during shutdown

The watcher started in searchSupport.init uses context.Background() and never checks whether the events channel was closed. On server.Stop the SQL backend cancels its poller and closes the events channel; this loop then receives nil and calls handleEvent(nil), which dereferences evt.Type and panics. Because this PR now initializes search at startup, this watcher is always running. Use the server's cancellable context and handle the channel-close case by returning.

Shared error variable races in index build errgroup

In searchSupport.init every goroutine in the errgroup assigns to the same outer err variable with `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and increments totalBatchesIndexed without synchronization. Concurrent builds race: one goroutine can overwrite another goroutine's error with nil before it is returned, so errgroup.Wait can report success even though an index failed to build. The batch counter is also unreliable. Use a local err inside each goroutine and protect the counter.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup removes alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs

The cleanup registered at lines 381 and 425 uses testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, but the test creates IDPs named "idp-alias-0" through "idp-alias-20". The cleanup therefore never removes the created providers and may also fail with a not-found error, leaking IDPs into the test realm and making subsequent tests order-dependent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache invalidation can compare the original IDP model with itself

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate detects changes by comparing the model returned from getById(model.getInternalId()) with the caller-supplied model. When the ORGANIZATION feature is disabled, createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel returns the cached IdentityProviderModel directly. If a caller uses the normal getById -> mutate -> update pattern, the cached model is mutated in place, so getById inside update returns the same object as model. In that case both comparisons see identical predicate state and identical organizationId, and login caches are not invalidated even when enabled/hideOnLogin/linkOnly/organization link changed. The stale getForLogin cache can continue returning the old login IDP set. The original state must be fetched from the delegate or copied before mutation.

getForLogin does not check organization invalidation

The new getForLogin cache only checks isInvalid(cacheKey). The analogous getByOrganization method checks both isInvalid(cacheKey) and isInvalid(orgId) because organization changes can affect the cached IDP result. For getForLogin(ORG_ONLY/ALL, organizationId), a cached per-organization IDP list can survive organization invalidation/removal. If the organization change unlinks or removes an IDP without going through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.update/remove, login pages for that organization keep using stale IDP IDs. The method should also fall back when organizationId is non-null and isInvalid(organizationId) is true.

remove can throw NPE for missing alias when cache key is invalid

remove(alias) now always loads storedIdp and then, when the alias cache key is invalid, calls registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp). If the alias does not exist, storedIdp is null and registerIDPInvalidation dereferences it, throwing NPE. The method contract says remove should return false when no IDP is found, so this path must null-check storedIdp before invalidating.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

Such classes will no longer compile, and classes already compiled against an older version will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when CryptoIntegration.detectProvider invokes order(). It should be declared as a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) so existing implementations continue to work.

false_positives.candidate:

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). CryptoIntegration.init throws IllegalStateException("Not able to load any cryptoProvider with the classLoader ...") when no CryptoProvider SPI file is discoverable by that specific classloader. As a result, creating an AuthzClient now fails outright in environments where META-INF/services is not visible to AuthzClient's classloader (shaded/relocated jars, OSGi, custom classloaders), even though building the client does not otherwise need crypto. Previously create() worked without any crypto provider. This also adds an unexpected global static side effect to a simple factory method and should be made resilient to a missing provider.

Core provider-selection change is untested

ECDSAAlgorithmTest only round-trips a signature through the new ASN1 encoder/decoder; it never exercises the feature this PR introduces. There is no test that places two CryptoProvider service implementations on the classpath and asserts the highest-order provider is selected, no test that the previous duplicate-provider failure is (or is not) still raised for equal orders, and no test that an authz client obtains a usable crypto provider through CryptoIntegration after ServiceLoader discovery. Given the detectProvider behavior change, the selection logic—the main risk of the PR—has no coverage.

Provider selection is non-deterministic when order() ties; fail-fast on duplicates removed

detectProvider now sorts discovered providers by CryptoProvider.order() descending and silently returns the first, removing the previous IllegalStateException thrown when more than one provider is on the classpath. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so whenever two of them are present (e.g. default crypto plus FIPS) the winner is decided solely by the non-deterministic ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order (the sort is stable), not by the order() value. In a FIPS deployment that can silently select the non-FIPS provider and downgrade cryptography, and genuine duplicate-provider misconfigurations that used to abort at startup now go unnoticed. The built-in providers need distinct deterministic order values, and equal-order duplicates should still fail rather than silently pick one.

getKeyStore ignores provider and cannot load non-JDK keystore formats

getKeyStore(format) uses KeyStore.getInstance(format.name()) against the default JVM security providers instead of going through a specific provider. On that runtime every q.shutdown call raises AttributeError (which is only logged), the blocked worker get() calls are never woken, and worker.join(timeout=5.0) is then called for each of the 20 workers. Shutdown can hang for roughly 100 seconds and leak daemon threads, and the new tests that call shutdown can time out.

Worker marks offsets complete even when processing fails

OrderedQueueWorker.run calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in a finally block. If result_processor raises, the exception is logged and the offset is still marked complete, so the commit loop commits past a failed message and it is never retried. This contradicts the strategy docstring guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing. The problem is worse in real use because ResultProcessor.__call__ catches its own exceptions, so failures look like success to the worker. The new test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling expects no commit for a failing message, but it stops 0.2s after processing, before the commit loop's 1s interval, so it does not catch this behavior.

Offset tracker can commit past a gap after the first commit

get_committable_offsets computes start = max(last_committed + 1, min(all_offsets)). After 100 is committed, mark_committed removes it, leaving all_offsets={102} if 101 was not submitted. start then becomes 102, and a completed 102 is committed without ever seeing 101. The tracker therefore does not actually block commits across a gap except while last_committed+1 is still inside the tracked set. This contradicts the documented guarantee and the intent of test_offset_gaps_block_commits/test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps; if 101 is expected to arrive later, it can be skipped.

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and passes that same object to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy returned by create_with_partitions. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close, which is called through join on partition revocation, calls queue_pool.shutdown(), permanently stopping the workers and queues. On a subsequent partition assignment the factory reuses the same shut-down pool, so submits go to a dead queue pool and offsets stop being committed. Factory.shutdown then calls shutdown again on the same object. Either create/dispose a pool per strategy, or do not tear down the factory-owned pool from the strategy's close.

Graceful shutdown exits workers before draining queued work

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). The worker loop condition is `while not self.shutdown`, so after finishing the current item a worker exits and never calls get() again; queued items are left unprocessed. The immediate=False drain semantics therefore never happen, and close abandons pending queued work while its offsets remain uncommitted. The stop flag should be set only after the queues have drained, or the worker loop should continue processing non-empty queues after shutdown is requested.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the doc claim

FixedQueuePool constructs queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit only calls put(), which never blocks. If one subscription is slow, its queue and OffsetTracker.all_offsets grow without bound while the consumer keeps polling, which can eventually OOM the consumer. The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing limits the queue depth or propagates pressure back to the consumer. `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor(getattr(item, self.key))`, but `organization_auditlogs.py` instantiates it with `order_by=-datetime`, so the value is a `datetime`. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError` as soon as `build_cursor` calls the key function on the first result. Its `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw cursor integer instead of converting it back to a datetime, so later pages would compare a datetime column with an integer. Any audit-log request with `optimized_pagination=true` and the required permission will 500 instead of paginating. The optimized paginator needs the datetime conversion used by `DateTimePaginator`, or the endpoint needs a compatible paginator.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor` on a `datetime` attribute (because `order_by` is `-datetime`), which raises a `TypeError`.

false_positives.candidate:
Span buffer keys change from Redis sets to sorted sets without migration

This line starts writing `span-buf:s:*` keys with `ZADD`, and the Lua script now uses `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE`/`ZPOPMIN` while `_load_segment_data` uses `ZSCAN`. The key namespace and TTLs are unchanged, so old workers and existing keys still contain Redis SETs created by `SADD`/`SSCAN`. During a rolling deploy, or for up to `redis_ttl` seconds of pre-existing keys, new workers will hit `WRONGTYPE` on SET keys and old workers will hit `WRONGTYPE` on ZSET keys. That aborts span ingestion and flushing and can drop spans. A versioned key prefix or a dual read/write migration is needed.

Eviction cap is hard-coded to 1000 and ignores max_segment_spans

The Lua eviction always keeps at most 1000 spans, while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` defaults to 1001 and is still accepted as a constructor argument. The Python-side `max_segment_spans` check was removed from `_load_segment_data`, so that setting is now a no-op: configuring a lower limit will not bound segment size, and the default behavior silently drops one span from a 1001-span segment instead of honoring the configured threshold. The cap should be passed into the script or enforced consistently in Python.

No test exercises the new >1000-span eviction path

All span-buffer tests in this file build segments of at most five spans, so the new `zpopmin` eviction branch is never executed. The hard-coded cap, interaction with `max_segment_spans`, cleanup of redirects and TTLs for evicted spans, and root-span retention under eviction are unverified. Add a test with more than 1000 spans in one segment and assert the intended survivors and key cleanup.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses outer dataset and original request query

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` and the actual `query` to execute, but it calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)`. `dataset` is the closure's original dataset, and the helper reads `request.GET['query']`, not the `query` argument. In the dashboard split path this method is invoked with `discover` plus synthesized `errors_only_query`/`transactions_only_query`; a generic query split into errors will not be upsampled, and a transaction-only split derived from a request containing `event.type:error` can be upsampled even though it targets transaction rows. This yields wrong counts and may query sample_weight for transaction data. Pass `scoped_dataset` and the actual query string into the eligibility check.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue directly identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer closure's `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`, which breaks upsampling during dashboard split paths where the query runs against `discover`. The candidate also notes an additional related issue with the query parameter, making it even more thorough.

false_positives.candidate:
Substring check treats negated and mixed event.type queries as error-only

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the raw query contains the substring `event.type:error`. A query such as `!event.type:error` (which excludes errors) or `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` is classified as error-only, so `count()` is rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` for transaction or mixed results. Transaction events have no meaningful sample_weight, so counts are understated or zero. The tests only cover exact positive and transaction-only examples and miss negation/OR cases.

upsampled_count drops events whose sample_weight is NULL

`upsampled_count` is implemented as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no coalesce/default. The new factory helper only sets a sample rate when `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` exists, and the code explicitly assumes every event has a sample_weight. Any event without a sample rate (older events, unsampled errors, or mixed projects after allowlisting) contributes NULL and is omitted from the sum instead of contributing 1, so allowlisted projects undercount errors. The tests only cover events that have client_sample_rate and would not catch this; the aggregate should use `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))` or equivalent.

Top-events ordering still uses unsampled count()

When `topEvents` is used, only `timeseries_columns` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()`. The `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` argument, including any default count ordering, still references the original `count()` aggregation, so Snuba selects the top N groups using raw counts while the response displays upsampled counts. With a large sample-rate skew the endpoint can return the wrong set of top events. The transformed aggregation needs to be applied to orderby/equations as well.

Accidental gitlink without .gitmodules

This PR adds a gitlink entry named `sentry-repo` pointing at the base commit, but no `.gitmodules` entry or URL is added. A checkout with submodule initialization will fail with `No url found for submodule path 'sentry-repo' in .gitmodules`, and the repository gets an unintended empty submodule. Remove this file/gitlink unless a submodule is genuinely intended.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and renderer collide on UID 0

The new denial-cache key is built from `checkReq.UserUID`, which for different identity types can be the same string. Anonymous subjects arrive as `anonymous:0` (UID `0`) and render-service subjects as `render:0` (UID `0`), so both produce the same key `namespace.perm_0_<action>_<name>_<parent>`. If an anonymous user is denied access to a dashboard (caching a denial under UID `0`), a renderer check for the same dashboard/action/folder within the 30s TTL takes the early `return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed:false}` at line 120 and is denied even though `getRendererPermissions` grants `*` for `dashboards:read`/`folders:read`. Consequence: image/PDF rendering intermittently fails to read dashboards whenever an anonymous denial was recently cached for the same resource. The key must include the identity type (and ideally use the resolved identity, not the raw subject UID).

Denial cache is not invalidated on permission changes, re-introducing the creator-lockout in a race

The denial is cached with `shortCacheTTL` (30s) and there is no hook to evict `permDenialCache` when permissions are granted (new dashboard/folder owned by creator, team/dashboard permission added, etc.). The PR's goal is to let a creator fetch a resource they just created; if the first `Check` for the new resource runs before the permission row is visible to `GetUserPermissions` (propagation/commit delay), that first check returns false and stores a denial keyed by the resource. The creator's retries are then served by the denial cache for up to 30s, so they still cannot access the newly created dashboard/folder during the window — the exact symptom being fixed. Consider invalidating denial entries on writes or using a much shorter TTL for denials of just-created resources.

Denial-cache write path and cache-served denial are untested

`TestService_CacheCheck`'s "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" seeds `permDenialCache` directly, so it only exercises the read path. Nothing verifies that a real denial (line 154 of service.go) writes to `permDenialCache`, nor that a second identical `Check` is subsequently answered from the denial cache without hitting the store (e.g., asserting `store.calls` stays constant on the second call). The new write path and the intended performance benefit are therefore unprotected against regressions.

permissionCacheUsage conflates the denial cache with the permission cache

The `permissionCacheUsage` metric is incremented on a denial-cache hit (line 118) as if it were a permission-cache hit, and on a permission-cache hit that ultimately denies the request it is recorded as `"false"` (line 137). Since the metric is meant to measure the permission cache, mixing in the new denial cache makes dashboards/alerts on cache effectiveness misleading (denial hits look like permission-cache hits, and permission-cache hits that deny look like misses). Consider a distinct counter for the denial cache or only recording permission-cache outcomes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when existing integration metadata has no "sender"

The user-match check reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. However, `build_integration` only writes `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, and none of the pipeline views bind `sender` (the happy-path test even asserts that the resulting metadata contains no `sender` key). This means integrations created by this very pipeline have no `sender` in metadata. Whenever such an ACTIVE integration exists without a remaining OrganizationIntegration (e.g. a re-install/re-link after the org integration row was removed, or an orphaned integration), this line raises `KeyError` and returns a 500 instead of the intended friendly failure page. It also means the new 'authenticated user == installer' protection can never apply to pipeline-created integrations. false_positives.candidate:
Uncaught exceptions from token exchange and get_user_info produce 500

`safe_urlopen(...)` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) are not wrapped in error handling. Only `safe_urlread`/`parse_qsl` are guarded. No test for the missing/invalid access_token failure path

The PR description lists 'GitHub could not generate correct access_token from the code (wrong or attempt of re-use of code)' as a required failure case, but no test covers the branch at line 431 where the token response contains no `access_token`. The new tests only exercise the happy path, state mismatch, and the user-mismatch path. Add a test that stubs the access_token endpoint to return no token (or an error body) and asserts the 'Invalid installation request.' failure page, since this is a stated security-relevant guarantee.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache invalidation can compare the original IDP model with itself

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate detects changes by comparing the model returned from getById(model.getInternalId()) with the caller-supplied model. When the ORGANIZATION feature is disabled, createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel returns the cached IdentityProviderModel directly. If a caller uses the normal getById -> mutate -> update pattern, the cached model is mutated in place, so getById inside update returns the same object as model. In that case both comparisons see identical predicate state and identical organizationId, and login caches are not invalidated even when enabled/hideOnLogin/linkOnly/organization link changed. The stale getForLogin cache can continue returning the old login IDP set. The original state must be fetched from the delegate or copied before mutation.

getForLogin does not check organization invalidation

The new getForLogin cache only checks isInvalid(cacheKey). The analogous getByOrganization method checks both isInvalid(cacheKey) and isInvalid(orgId) because organization changes can affect the cached IDP result. For getForLogin(ORG_ONLY/ALL, organizationId), a cached per-organization IDP list can survive organization invalidation/removal. If the organization change unlinks or removes an IDP without going through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.update/remove, login pages for that organization keep using stale IDP IDs. The method should also fall back when organizationId is non-null and isInvalid(organizationId) is true.

remove can throw NPE for missing alias when cache key is invalid

remove(alias) now always loads storedIdp and then, when the alias cache key is invalid, calls registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp). If the alias does not exist, storedIdp is null and registerIDPInvalidation dereferences it, throwing NPE. The method contract says remove should return false when no IDP is found, so this path must null-check storedIdp before invalidating.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

After the read-lock fast path misses, the function takes the write lock and unconditionally re-reads/re-parses the manifest (readWebAssetsFromFile) and republishes the cache, without re-checking entryPointAssetsCache. On a cold start, N goroutines can all observe the cache as nil under RLock, then serialize on the write lock and each perform a full file open + JSON decode of assets-manifest.json even though the first one already populated the cache. The consequence is redundant sequential I/O and CPU per waiter (a thundering herd) right at startup. Re-check `if entryPointAssetsCache != nil` (for non-dev env) immediately after acquiring the write lock to avoid this.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: an incomplete double-checked locking pattern where the cache is checked under a read lock, and upon missing, a write lock is acquired without re-checking if another goroutine populated the cache in the meantime.

false_positives.candidate:
Write lock is held during blocking I/O

The exclusive lock (taken at line 48 and held via defer until return) covers the entire manifest read, including readWebAssetsFromFile (file open + JSON decode) and, when the CDN path is enabled, readWebAssetsFromCDN (an HTTP GET with the request context). While the writer holds the lock, all other GetWebAssets callers block on RLock, so slow disk or a slow/hanging CDN response stalls every concurrent request. In dev mode this happens on every call. A better structure is to build the result outside the lock and only hold the write lock briefly to publish it, or use sync.Once for the non-dev path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

The cleanup loop runs every cleanup job, including temporary file cleanup, snapshot deletion, dashboard-version deletion, image cleanup, short URL cleanup, query-history cleanup, and annotation cleanup. false_positives.candidate:
MaxCount cleanup can delete beyond the configured retention count under concurrent deletes

In the MaxCount branch, the IDs to delete are selected with LIMIT/OFFSET in one statement and deleted by ID in a separate, non-transactional statement. If annotations among the newest cfg.MaxCount rows are deleted between the SELECT and DELETE (for example by a user deleting an annotation or by another cleanup process), the OFFSET window shifts. IDs that were outside the protected set at SELECT time can then be inside the newest MaxCount rows, but the DELETE still removes them, leaving fewer than MaxCount annotations and losing data beyond the configured retention policy. The previous DELETE-with-subquery made the selection and deletion atomic for this purpose. Revalidate the offset in the DELETE or otherwise make the two steps atomic/guarded.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete metric uses object name as kind label

Delete records a successful storage duration with d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object name where the kind label belongs. This mislabels every successful delete metric and creates unbounded cardinailty/corrupted kind grouping. It should pass options.Kind like the other metric calls.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: passing `name` instead of `options.Kind` when recording metrics, which is inconsistent with other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Storage failures recorded as legacy metric

In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). No legacy call has happened, so this records the storage failure and storage duration under the legacy metric. Update has the same bug at line 129. These should call recordStorageDuration instead; otherwise storage error/latency dashboards are wrong and legacy failure counts are inflated.

Async legacy writes can be canceled by request context

All write methods start their background legacy call with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) where ctx is the original HTTP request context. The server cancels that context when the request handler returns, which can happen immediately after the method returns while the goroutine is still starting. The derived context is canceled too, so the legacy fallback write can be skipped or fail spuriously. The same pattern occurs in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a fresh background context with only the needed values.

Independent async writes can reorder legacy state

Each write launches an independent goroutine with no per-object sequencing. A rapid create/update/delete sequence for the same object can reach LegacyStorage out of order, e.g. a delete may complete before an earlier update and leave the object deleted in unified but still present in legacy, or an older update may overwrite a newer one in legacy. Because reads only use unified storage, this divergence goes unnoticed until fallback is needed. Legacy writes need serialization per object (queue/worker) or another ordering guarantee.

Legacy Update no longer uses the object produced by unified storage

The old implementation wrapped objInfo so LegacyStorage.Update received the exact object returned by Storage.Update. The new implementation passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update, so LegacyStorage recomputes UpdatedObject against its own copy. If that copy is stale because prior asynchronous writes have not landed, or if unified storage defaulted/mutated fields, legacy can store a different object than unified storage, defeating the fallback guarantee. Capture res from Storage.Update and pass a wrapper using that object to Legacy.Update.

Legacy write failures are no longer logged

The background legacy Create path records only a metric and does not log errObjectSt. The same is true for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Previously legacy failures were logged with object and error details. Now a failed fallback write is invisible in logs, making production diagnosis much harder.

Delete tests do not mock or wait for async legacy call

TestMode3_Delete success configures only Storage.Delete, but Mode3.Delete now asynchronously invokes Legacy.Delete. There is no legacy mock expectation, so testify's mock panics with an unexpected call if the goroutine runs. TestMode3_DeleteCollection has the same issue at line 284. More generally, none of the Mode3 unit tests wait for the background goroutine, so they can pass without exercising the legacy write path and can panic or race nondeterministically. The tests should set up the legacy mock, synchronize on the goroutine, and assert the legacy call.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume synchronous legacy writes

The new file and unified-storage mode 3 subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately reads /api/playlists after k8s create/update/delete and asserts the legacy API already reflects the change. Mode 3 performs those legacy writes asynchronously, so the legacy request can race ahead of the background write and make these tests flaky. The mode 3 cases need an eventually/retry check for legacy consistency or should not assert immediate legacy state.

false_positives.candidate:
New fallback behavior ships with no tests

This PR changes core translation resolution (custom `I18n.fallbacks`, on-demand loading of the fallback chain, removal of Rails' `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` in production/profile/cloud66) but adds no tests. The behavior is subtle and easy to regress: fallback ordering (user locale -> SiteSetting.default_locale -> :en), deduplication, behavior when the default locale is unavailable, and the interaction with the LRU cache in `I18n.translate` are all untested. A maintainer cannot verify that `I18n.t` for a key missing in the current locale now returns the default-locale/en string (and that missing keys still raise/return 'translation missing' when nothing exists). Add specs for these paths.

Fallback locales are only preloaded inside controller requests

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is invoked only from `ApplicationController#set_locale`, so the fallback chain (current locale, `SiteSetting.default_locale`, `:en`) is loaded only during web requests. Outside requests — background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console — `I18n.translate` (lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb:68) loads only `config.locale`, and the `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` translation path calls `super` for fallback locales without triggering `load_locale` for them. Result: in those contexts a key missing from the active locale may resolve to 'translation missing' instead of the intended default-locale/`:en` string, because those locale files were never loaded in that process. Loading the fallback chain should happen centrally (e.g., in the patched `I18n.translate`/`ensure_loaded!`, or an initializer), not solely in a controller filter.

Inconsistent and fragile backend include target for fallbacks

Pluralization is mixed into `I18n::Backend::Simple` directly (line 5), but fallbacks are mixed into `I18n.backend.class` (line 9). This forces eager instantiation of `I18n.backend` at initializer time and, more importantly, means fallbacks are only attached to whichever backend class happens to be active during this initializer. If `I18n.backend` is later replaced (e.g., by a Chain backend in some environment or a future change), the `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` module silently drops off and fallbacks stop working with no error. Use the same explicit `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` form used for pluralization (or otherwise guarantee the included backend is the one actually used).

FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but only overrides `[]`, breaking standard Fallbacks API

`I18n.fallbacks` is normally an `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks`, which exposes `[]`, `[]=`, `key?`, `fetch`, `each`, `to_h`, `defaults`, etc. `FallbackLocaleList < Hash` stores no keys and only overrides `[]`, so any code (current or in future i18n gem internals) that iterates `I18n.fallbacks`, checks `key?`, or relies on the stored mapping will see an empty Hash and behave incorrectly. Subclass `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` and override `[]` instead, so the object remains a real fallbacks collection while still customizing the chain.

The desktop equivalent was correctly changed to primary 20% / secondary 80%; mobile should match with `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 80%))`. As-is, the mobile h3 headings are visually de-emphasized compared with the previous design.

It should use the same complementary pattern, e.g. `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`.

For a blocked address both calls run this validator, so one signup attempt increments `match_count` twice, and any repeated `valid?` call also writes to the database. Validation should be side-effect free; record the match when the rejection is actually handled, or otherwise ensure it is counted once.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

On PostgreSQL, `bad@spam.com` and `Bad@Spam.com` are different values, so a blocked address can be used again simply by changing capitalization. RSS item HTML is imported raw without sanitization

`poll_feed` passes `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` straight to `TopicEmbed.import`, which creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. `TopicEmbed.import` does not sanitize `contents`, and `app/views/embed/best.html.erb:19` renders `raw post.cooked`. Non-atomic SETNX/EXPIRE can permanently throttle an embed URL

`retrieved_recently?` calls `$redis.setnx` and then a separate `$redis.expire`. If the process dies between those two calls, the key is left without a TTL, so every subsequent attempt for that URL sees it as retrieved and never performs retrieval again. Use an atomic `SET key value EX 60 NX` (or a MULTI/EXEC) so the throttle cannot become permanent.

Protocol-relative URLs are rewritten as root-relative

The `start_with?('/')` checks at lines 64 and 70 also match protocol-relative URLs such as `//cdn.example.com/a.png`. The code then strips all leading slashes and prefixes the feed host, producing `http://feedhost/cdn.example.com/a.png`, which is wrong and breaks links or images in imported content. Only prefix when there is exactly one leading slash and the URL is not protocol-relative.

true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: hardcoding the 10 MB limit instead of using `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, which causes client/server divergence and also affects the 413 error handler.

false_positives.candidate:
In-place image downsize can corrupt the uploaded file on failure

The new auto-downsize code calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)`, overwriting the original upload file in place, and ignores the boolean return value. If ImageMagick/gifsicle fails partway through (unsupported or malformed image, missing delegate, killed process), the destination path may already be truncated or partially written. The loop then retries on the damaged file up to five times before `Upload.create_for` stores whatever remains, so a failed resize can turn a valid upload into a corrupt or empty file. The resize should write to a separate temporary path and atomically replace the original only on success, and the caller should stop/fail when conversion returns false.

Animated GIF detection uses the tempfile path and strips animation

`OptimizedImage.optimize` decides whether to use the animated conversion path by checking `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. The controller passes `tempfile.path` as `from`; Rack upload tempfile paths normally have no `.gif` extension, even when the uploaded filename is `.gif`. As a result `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` has no effect for normal uploads: a large animated GIF falls back to `convert from[0]`, which keeps only the first frame. The original upload then loses its animation (or the conversion fails). Animated handling should be based on the original filename/content type, not the tempfile path.

Five fixed 80% passes may leave the image above max_image_size_kb

The resize loop runs at most five times and then proceeds without checking whether the file is now within `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. Five 80% linear resizes reduce area to roughly 10.7%, so a 10 MB image can remain above a 1 MB limit; for smaller configured limits the gap is larger. In that case `Upload.create_for` receives an oversized file and the upload either fails server-side validation or, if validation does not enforce this path, stores an image larger than the configured limit. The loop should verify the final size and fail explicitly if the target cannot be reached.

No tests cover the automatic image downsize path

The PR adds a new server-side resize path and a new `OptimizedImage.downsize` overload but does not add tests. There is no coverage for oversized image reduction, non-image uploads, conversion failure behavior, or animated GIF handling. Those are exactly the paths where the in-place mutation and animation-detection issues above can regress unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

false_positives.candidate:
Direct tu.save! bypasses TopicUser.change and leaves notifications_reason_id nil

The unsubscribe action mutates the notification level with `tu.notification_level = ...; tu.save!` instead of `TopicUser.change` (which `set_notifications` uses). `TopicUser.change` sets `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id = :user_changed`, and publishes the change on MessageBus. So the user unsubscribes, then normal reading silently re-subscribes them — the feature does not stick. It also skips the MessageBus publish, so an open client won't reflect the new level.

Rails CSRF protection only covers non-GET requests, and this action additionally does `skip_before_filter :check_xhr`. The permission should be restricted to the organizer and authorized team admins/owners unless attendee self-service is explicitly intended and protected.

The handler builds `EventManager` from `ctx.user` via `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `{ ...user, credentials }`. When a team admin/owner or attendee invokes the mutation, this attempts to update the organizer's calendar using the caller's credentials. That can fail or update the wrong account even though the guests have already been persisted in the database. It should load and use the booking organizer's credentials for the calendar operation.

Guests are persisted before external calendar update can fail

The Prisma update inserts the new attendees before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` runs. If the calendar update throws, the mutation fails and the caller sees an error, but the guest rows remain in the booking without the corresponding calendar update (and before any emails). This leaves booking data and external calendars inconsistent. The operation needs failure handling or a rollback path.

After a failed validation, `isInvalidEmail` is set to true, but the success handler closes the dialog and only resets `multiEmailValue`; it never calls `setIsInvalidEmail(false)`. This adds a security-sensitive mutation with authorization, deduplication, blacklist filtering, calendar update, and email behavior, but no tests are included. At minimum, tests should cover organizer vs team admin vs attendee permissions, duplicate/blacklisted email filtering, passing only actually-added guests to the email sender, and the error path when the calendar update fails.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

Adding `int order();` as an abstract method to the public CryptoProvider interface is a source- and binary-incompatible change for every third-party CryptoProvider implementation (custom providers, and the keycloak-client repo this code is later synced to). Such classes will no longer compile, and classes already compiled against an older version will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when CryptoIntegration.detectProvider invokes order(). false_positives.candidate:
Provider selection is non-deterministic when order() ties; fail-fast on duplicates removed

detectProvider now sorts discovered providers by CryptoProvider.order() descending and silently returns the first, removing the previous IllegalStateException thrown when more than one provider is on the classpath. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so whenever two of them are present (e.g. default crypto plus FIPS) the winner is decided solely by the non-deterministic ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order (the sort is stable), not by the order() value. In a FIPS deployment that can silently select the non-FIPS provider and downgrade cryptography, and genuine duplicate-provider misconfigurations that used to abort at startup now go unnoticed. The built-in providers need distinct deterministic order values, and equal-order duplicates should still fail rather than silently pick one.

AuthzClient.create now throws if no CryptoProvider is discoverable by its classloader

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). CryptoIntegration.init throws IllegalStateException("Not able to load any cryptoProvider with the classLoader ...") when no CryptoProvider SPI file is discoverable by that specific classloader. As a result, creating an AuthzClient now fails outright in environments where META-INF/services is not visible to AuthzClient's classloader (shaded/relocated jars, OSGi, custom classloaders), even though building the client does not otherwise need crypto. Previously create() worked without any crypto provider. This also adds an unexpected global static side effect to a simple factory method and should be made resilient to a missing provider.

ECDSAAlgorithmTest only round-trips a signature through the new ASN1 encoder/decoder; it never exercises the feature this PR introduces. There is no test that places two CryptoProvider service implementations on the classpath and asserts the highest-order provider is selected, no test that the previous duplicate-provider failure is (or is not) still raised for equal orders, and no test that an authz client obtains a usable crypto provider through CryptoIntegration after ServiceLoader discovery. Given the detectProvider behavior change, the selection logic—the main risk of the PR—has no coverage.

getKeyStore ignores provider and cannot load non-JDK keystore formats

getKeyStore(format) uses KeyStore.getInstance(format.name()) against the default JVM security providers instead of going through a specific provider. For formats the JDK does not ship (e.g. BCFKS, BKS, PEM) this throws KeyStoreException, so CryptoProvider.getSupportedKeyStoreTypes()/getKeyStore() will claim formats this provider cannot actually load, since the authz-client has no BouncyCastle on the classpath. On that runtime every q.shutdown call raises AttributeError (which is only logged), the blocked worker get() calls are never woken, and worker.join(timeout=5.0) is then called for each of the 20 workers. Shutdown can hang for roughly 100 seconds and leak daemon threads, and the new tests that call shutdown can time out.

Worker marks offsets complete even when processing fails
