If result_processor raises, the exception is logged and the offset is still marked complete, so the commit loop commits past a failed message and it is never retried. This contradicts the strategy docstring guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing. The problem is worse in real use because ResultProcessor.__call__ catches its own exceptions, so failures look like success to the worker. The new test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling expects no commit for a failing message, but it stops 0.2s after processing, before the commit loop's 1s interval, so it does not catch this behavior.

Offset tracker can commit past a gap after the first commit

get_committable_offsets computes start = max(last_committed + 1, min(all_offsets)). After 100 is committed, mark_committed removes it, leaving all_offsets={102} if 101 was not submitted. start then becomes 102, and a completed 102 is committed without ever seeing 101. The tracker therefore does not actually block commits across a gap except while last_committed+1 is still inside the tracked set. This contradicts the documented guarantee and the intent of test_offset_gaps_block_commits/test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps; if 101 is expected to arrive later, it can be skipped.

Strategy close permanently shuts down the factory-owned shared queue pool

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and passes that same object to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy returned by create_with_partitions. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close, which is called through join on partition revocation, calls queue_pool.shutdown(), permanently stopping the workers and queues. On a subsequent partition assignment the factory reuses the same shut-down pool, so submits go to a dead queue pool and offsets stop being committed. Factory.shutdown then calls shutdown again on the same object. Either create/dispose a pool per strategy, or do not tear down the factory-owned pool from the strategy's close.

Graceful shutdown exits workers before draining queued work

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). The worker loop condition is `while not self.shutdown`, so after finishing the current item a worker exits and never calls get() again; queued items are left unprocessed. The immediate=False drain semantics therefore never happen, and close abandons pending queued work while its offsets remain uncommitted. The stop flag should be set only after the queues have drained, or the worker loop should continue processing non-empty queues after shutdown is requested.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the doc claim

FixedQueuePool constructs queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit only calls put(), which never blocks. If one subscription is slow, its queue and OffsetTracker.all_offsets grow without bound while the consumer keeps polling, which can eventually OOM the consumer. The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing limits the queue depth or propagates pressure back to the consumer. Use bounded queues and/or block or stop polling when total queued work exceeds a threshold.

Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage metric

Legacy latency/failures are therefore attributed to unified storage, and the legacy metric is never updated. It should call recordLegacyDuration.

The derived context is canceled too, so the legacy fallback write can be skipped or fail spuriously. The same pattern occurs in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). Each write launches an independent goroutine with no per-object sequencing. If that copy is stale because prior asynchronous writes have not landed, or if unified storage defaulted/mutated fields, legacy can store a different object than unified storage, defeating the fallback guarantee. false_positives.candidate:
New fallback behavior ships with no tests

This PR changes core translation resolution (custom `I18n.fallbacks`, on-demand loading of the fallback chain, removal of Rails' `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` in production/profile/cloud66) but adds no tests. The behavior is subtle and easy to regress: fallback ordering (user locale -> SiteSetting.default_locale -> :en), deduplication, behavior when the default locale is unavailable, and the interaction with the LRU cache in `I18n.translate` are all untested. A maintainer cannot verify that `I18n.t` for a key missing in the current locale now returns the default-locale/en string (and that missing keys still raise/return 'translation missing' when nothing exists). Add specs for these paths.

Fallback locales are only preloaded inside controller requests

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is invoked only from `ApplicationController#set_locale`, so the fallback chain (current locale, `SiteSetting.default_locale`, `:en`) is loaded only during web requests. Outside requests — background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console — `I18n.translate` (lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb:68) loads only `config.locale`, and the `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` translation path calls `super` for fallback locales without triggering `load_locale` for them. Result: in those contexts a key missing from the active locale may resolve to 'translation missing' instead of the intended default-locale/`:en` string, because those locale files were never loaded in that process. Loading the fallback chain should happen centrally (e.g., in the patched `I18n.translate`/`ensure_loaded!`, or an initializer), not solely in a controller filter.

Inconsistent and fragile backend include target for fallbacks

Pluralization is mixed into `I18n::Backend::Simple` directly (line 5), but fallbacks are mixed into `I18n.backend.class` (line 9). This forces eager instantiation of `I18n.backend` at initializer time and, more importantly, means fallbacks are only attached to whichever backend class happens to be active during this initializer. If `I18n.backend` is later replaced (e.g., by a Chain backend in some environment or a future change), the `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` module silently drops off and fallbacks stop working with no error. Use the same explicit `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` form used for pluralization (or otherwise guarantee the included backend is the one actually used).

FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but only overrides `[]`, breaking standard Fallbacks API

`I18n.fallbacks` is normally an `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks`, which exposes `[]`, `[]=`, `key?`, `fetch`, `each`, `to_h`, `defaults`, etc. `FallbackLocaleList < Hash` stores no keys and only overrides `[]`, so any code (current or in future i18n gem internals) that iterates `I18n.fallbacks`, checks `key?`, or relies on the stored mapping will see an empty Hash and behave incorrectly. Subclass `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` and override `[]` instead, so the object remains a real fallbacks collection while still customizing the chain.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
In-place image downsize can corrupt the uploaded file on failure

The new auto-downsize code calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)`, overwriting the original upload file in place, and ignores the boolean return value. If ImageMagick/gifsicle fails partway through (unsupported or malformed image, missing delegate, killed process), the destination path may already be truncated or partially written. The loop then retries on the damaged file up to five times before `Upload.create_for` stores whatever remains, so a failed resize can turn a valid upload into a corrupt or empty file. The resize should write to a separate temporary path and atomically replace the original only on success, and the caller should stop/fail when conversion returns false.

Animated GIF detection uses the tempfile path and strips animation

`OptimizedImage.optimize` decides whether to use the animated conversion path by checking `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. The controller passes `tempfile.path` as `from`; Rack upload tempfile paths normally have no `.gif` extension, even when the uploaded filename is `.gif`. As a result `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` has no effect for normal uploads: a large animated GIF falls back to `convert from[0]`, which keeps only the first frame. The original upload then loses its animation (or the conversion fails). Animated handling should be based on the original filename/content type, not the tempfile path.

The resize loop runs at most five times and then proceeds without checking whether the file is now within `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. In that case `Upload.create_for` receives an oversized file and the upload either fails server-side validation or, if validation does not enforce this path, stores an image larger than the configured limit. The loop should verify the final size and fail explicitly if the target cannot be reached.

There is no coverage for oversized image reduction, non-image uploads, conversion failure behavior, or animated GIF handling. A Response serializes to {} in JSON, so the stored credential key is destroyed and all HubSpot calls fail. In the non-sharing path the refresh function returned a parsed HubspotToken, so the two return types are incompatible.

Zoho Bigin sharing path crashes reading .data on a Response

When credential sharing is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response; in the non-sharing path it returns the axios response that has .data. This code then evaluates tokenInfo.data.error, so in sharing mode tokenInfo.data is undefined and the property access throws a TypeError, breaking token refresh entirely. The two branches return incompatible types and the feature does not work for Bigin.

Zoho CRM sharing path crashes reading .data on a Response

With credential sharing enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, but this code expects the axios result and reads zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error. In sharing mode .data is undefined, so the property access throws a TypeError and token refresh is broken. Non-sharing returns the axios response (with .data), so the two paths are type-incompatible.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !==

The incoming CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET header is compared to process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET with !==. String inequality short-circuits at the first differing byte, leaking timing information about the expected secret and enabling a timing side-channel to guess it. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers). Also note the header name is looked up case-sensitively from process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME; since Node lowercases incoming header names, a non-lowercase value makes every request fail with 403.

The findFirst followed by create/update is not atomic. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same (userId, appId) can both observe no existing credential and both insert one, producing duplicate Credential rows (the schema does not enforce uniqueness on userId+appId). Use a unique constraint with upsert, or otherwise serialize per user/app.

Updating credentials does not reset the invalid flag

When updating an existing credential only key is written; the invalid flag is left untouched. Services such as GoogleCalendarService mark a credential invalid: true on invalid_grant, so a credential that was previously invalidated stays invalid even after fresh synced keys are written, and the app remains disabled. Reset invalid: false in the update.

The author states no tests were added and local tests were not run. This PR introduces a new authenticated endpoint that decrypts and writes credentials, plus a refresh-routing layer whose return type is inconsistent across callers. A single test exercising the sharing path would have caught the Response-vs-parsed-object mismatches in the Google/HubSpot/Zoho services.

On that runtime every q.shutdown call raises AttributeError (which is only logged), the blocked worker get() calls are never woken, and worker.join(timeout=5.0) is then called for each of the 20 workers. Shutdown can hang for roughly 100 seconds and leak daemon threads, and the new tests that call shutdown can time out.

Worker marks offsets complete even when processing fails

OrderedQueueWorker.run calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in a finally block. If result_processor raises, the exception is logged and the offset is still marked complete, so the commit loop commits past a failed message and it is never retried. This contradicts the strategy docstring guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing. The problem is worse in real use because ResultProcessor.__call__ catches its own exceptions, so failures look like success to the worker. The new test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling expects no commit for a failing message, but it stops 0.2s after processing, before the commit loop's 1s interval, so it does not catch this behavior.

Offset tracker can commit past a gap after the first commit

get_committable_offsets computes start = max(last_committed + 1, min(all_offsets)). After 100 is committed, mark_committed removes it, leaving all_offsets={102} if 101 was not submitted. start then becomes 102, and a completed 102 is committed without ever seeing 101. The tracker therefore does not actually block commits across a gap except while last_committed+1 is still inside the tracked set. This contradicts the documented guarantee and the intent of test_offset_gaps_block_commits/test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps; if 101 is expected to arrive later, it can be skipped.

Strategy close permanently shuts down the factory-owned shared queue pool

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and passes that same object to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy returned by create_with_partitions. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close, which is called through join on partition revocation, calls queue_pool.shutdown(), permanently stopping the workers and queues. On a subsequent partition assignment the factory reuses the same shut-down pool, so submits go to a dead queue pool and offsets stop being committed. Factory.shutdown then calls shutdown again on the same object. Either create/dispose a pool per strategy, or do not tear down the factory-owned pool from the strategy's close.

Graceful shutdown exits workers before draining queued work

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). The worker loop condition is `while not self.shutdown`, so after finishing the current item a worker exits and never calls get() again; queued items are left unprocessed. The immediate=False drain semantics therefore never happen, and close abandons pending queued work while its offsets remain uncommitted. The stop flag should be set only after the queues have drained, or the worker loop should continue processing non-empty queues after shutdown is requested.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the doc claim

FixedQueuePool constructs queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit only calls put(), which never blocks. If one subscription is slow, its queue and OffsetTracker.all_offsets grow without bound while the consumer keeps polling, which can eventually OOM the consumer. The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing limits the queue depth or propagates pressure back to the consumer. Use bounded queues and/or block or stop polling when total queued work exceeds a threshold.

If that copy is stale because prior asynchronous writes have not landed, or if unified storage defaulted/mutated fields, legacy can store a different object than unified storage, defeating the fallback guarantee. Capture res from Storage.Update and pass a wrapper using that object to Legacy.Update.

Legacy write failures are no longer logged

The background legacy Create path records only a metric and does not log errObjectSt. The same is true for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Previously legacy failures were logged with object and error details. Now a failed fallback write is invisible in logs, making production diagnosis much harder.

More generally, none of the Mode3 unit tests wait for the background goroutine, so they can pass without exercising the legacy write path and can panic or race nondeterministically. The behavior is subtle and easy to regress: fallback ordering (user locale -> SiteSetting.default_locale -> :en), deduplication, behavior when the default locale is unavailable, and the interaction with the LRU cache in `I18n.translate` are all untested. A maintainer cannot verify that `I18n.t` for a key missing in the current locale now returns the default-locale/en string (and that missing keys still raise/return 'translation missing' when nothing exists). Fallback locales are only preloaded inside controller requests

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is invoked only from `ApplicationController#set_locale`, so the fallback chain (current locale, `SiteSetting.default_locale`, `:en`) is loaded only during web requests. Outside requests — background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console — `I18n.translate` (lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb:68) loads only `config.locale`, and the `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` translation path calls `super` for fallback locales without triggering `load_locale` for them. Result: in those contexts a key missing from the active locale may resolve to 'translation missing' instead of the intended default-locale/`:en` string, because those locale files were never loaded in that process. Loading the fallback chain should happen centrally (e.g., in the patched `I18n.translate`/`ensure_loaded!`, or an initializer), not solely in a controller filter.

Pluralization is mixed into `I18n::Backend::Simple` directly (line 5), but fallbacks are mixed into `I18n.backend.class` (line 9). This forces eager instantiation of `I18n.backend` at initializer time and, more importantly, means fallbacks are only attached to whichever backend class happens to be active during this initializer. If `I18n.backend` is later replaced (e.g., by a Chain backend in some environment or a future change), the `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` module silently drops off and fallbacks stop working with no error. Use the same explicit `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` form used for pluralization (or otherwise guarantee the included backend is the one actually used).

`I18n.fallbacks` is normally an `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks`, which exposes `[]`, `[]=`, `key?`, `fetch`, `each`, `to_h`, `defaults`, etc. `FallbackLocaleList < Hash` stores no keys and only overrides `[]`, so any code (current or in future i18n gem internals) that iterates `I18n.fallbacks`, checks `key?`, or relies on the stored mapping will see an empty Hash and behave incorrectly. false_positives.candidate:

The new auto-downsize code calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)`, overwriting the original upload file in place, and ignores the boolean return value. If ImageMagick/gifsicle fails partway through (unsupported or malformed image, missing delegate, killed process), the destination path may already be truncated or partially written. The loop then retries on the damaged file up to five times before `Upload.create_for` stores whatever remains, so a failed resize can turn a valid upload into a corrupt or empty file. The resize should write to a separate temporary path and atomically replace the original only on success, and the caller should stop/fail when conversion returns false.

Animated GIF detection uses the tempfile path and strips animation

`OptimizedImage.optimize` decides whether to use the animated conversion path by checking `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. The controller passes `tempfile.path` as `from`; Rack upload tempfile paths normally have no `.gif` extension, even when the uploaded filename is `.gif`. As a result `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` has no effect for normal uploads: a large animated GIF falls back to `convert from[0]`, which keeps only the first frame. The original upload then loses its animation (or the conversion fails). Animated handling should be based on the original filename/content type, not the tempfile path.

The resize loop runs at most five times and then proceeds without checking whether the file is now within `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. Five 80% linear resizes reduce area to roughly 10.7%, so a 10 MB image can remain above a 1 MB limit; for smaller configured limits the gap is larger. In that case `Upload.create_for` receives an oversized file and the upload either fails server-side validation or, if validation does not enforce this path, stores an image larger than the configured limit. The loop should verify the final size and fail explicitly if the target cannot be reached.

The PR adds a new server-side resize path and a new `OptimizedImage.downsize` overload but does not add tests. There is no coverage for oversized image reduction, non-image uploads, conversion failure behavior, or animated GIF handling. Those are exactly the paths where the in-place mutation and animation-detection issues above can regress unnoticed.

Reset the dialog state on both success and any close path.

No tests cover the new add-guests mutation

This adds a security-sensitive mutation with authorization, deduplication, blacklist filtering, calendar update, and email behavior, but no tests are included. At minimum, tests should cover organizer vs team admin vs attendee permissions, duplicate/blacklisted email filtering, passing only actually-added guests to the email sender, and the error path when the calendar update fails.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

Consuming a backup code does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes))`, finds the index, sets `backupCodes[index] = null`, then writes the whole re-encrypted array back. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both read the pre-consumption array, both find the code, and both write — resulting in the code being accepted twice (and the two writes clobbering each other). Since the guaranteed single-use property is the core security promise of backup codes, this should be made atomic (e.g., a conditional update / transaction) rather than a read-then-write.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: backup codes are decrypted, modified in memory and written back without atomicity. Concurrent logins with the same code could both succeed, which breaks single-use semantics.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-codes object URL is never revoked on unmount

`setBackupCodesUrl(URL.createObjectURL(textBlob))` creates an object URL that is only revoked on a subsequent `handleSetup` call. If the user closes the dialog (or the component unmounts) the blob URL leaks. The URL should be revoked in a cleanup effect on unmount.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem: the object URL created for the backup codes is never revoked when the component unmounts, so it leaks memory. The candidate also proposes the same fix, a cleanup effect that revokes the URL on unmount.

false_positives.candidate:
2FA users without backup codes have no way to obtain them

Any user who enabled 2FA before this PR has `backupCodes = NULL`. If they click "Lost access" and try to log in with a backup code, `authorize` throws `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes`, and the login UI shows the message "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." However there is no way to (re)generate backup codes once 2FA is already enabled: `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup` returns `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` when `user.twoFactorEnabled` is true. These existing users therefore hit a permanent dead end, and the guidance in the message is false. A regeneration path (or disabling/re-enabling) is needed before this is safe to ship.

Dismissing dialog after enable skips onEnable()

Previously `handleEnable` called `onEnable()` immediately on success. Now it only advances to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, and `onEnable()` is called solely from the "Close" button. If the user enables 2FA and then dismisses the dialog via the X button, overlay click, or Escape (`onOpenChange`), `onEnable()` is never invoked and `resetState()` never runs. The parent settings page is not notified that 2FA is now enabled, so the two-factor switch stays visually off while the account actually has 2FA active. The `onOpenChange` handler should invoke `onEnable()` when the flow had reached the post-enable backup-code step (and reset state).

No test coverage for backup code login or one-time consumption

The added e2e work only asserts that the download/copy/close buttons appear on the backup-code screen (with `// TODO: check file content` and `// TODO: check clipboard content`), and the header even notes `// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup`. The core new behavior — logging in with a backup code via "Lost access", the one-time deletion of the consumed code, `MissingBackupCodes`/`IncorrectBackupCode` handling, and disabling 2FA with a backup code — is entirely untested. The PR checklist itself states "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective." The most bug-prone logic (code consumption/concurrency) is unverified.

Copy success toast shown without awaiting clipboard write

`navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` returns a promise that is neither awaited nor caught, and the "backup codes copied!" success toast is fired unconditionally. In non-secure contexts or when clipboard permission is denied the write rejects silently while the user is told the copy succeeded — dangerous here because backup codes are shown once. The toast (and the e2e assertion on `toast-success`) should only fire after the write resolves.

tabIndex={-1} makes password visibility toggle keyboard-inaccessible for all PasswordFields

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide-password button removes it from the tab order for every `PasswordField` in the app, not just the two-factor modals this PR targets. Keyboard-only users can no longer reach the toggle, which is an accessibility regression. If the intent was only to prevent a specific form-submit issue, it should be scoped rather than applied to the shared component.

false_positives.candidate:
Google Meet fallback dereferences undefined destination calendar

After destinationCalendar became an array, `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` yields undefined when the event has no destination calendar. The next line still reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` whenever the location is MeetLocationType. Any Google Meet event without a destination calendar now throws a TypeError instead of falling back to Cal Video. Guard the access or use optional chaining.

Video booking references lose credentialId

In create(), referencesToCreate now sets `credentialId` only for calendar results (`isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`). Video results previously kept `result.credentialId`. Without a credentialId on the video booking reference, handleCancelBooking's video cancellation branch (`if (bookingVideoReference && bookingVideoReference.credentialId)`) is skipped, so the video meeting is not deleted when the booking is cancelled. Preserve `result.credentialId` for non-calendar results.

externalId is dropped before creating calendar events

createEvent now accepts an externalId argument, and EventManager passes `destination.externalId` so each destination should create its event on that calendar. But this call still invokes `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)` and never forwards externalId; it only copies externalId into the returned result. Google uses credentialId to pick the right destination, but Office365, Lark and BaseCalendarService all read `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. For a collective event with multiple hosts, every service call therefore uses the first host's calendar: the second Office365/Lark event fails or is created in the wrong calendar, and CalDAV silently creates nothing. Pass the destination externalId or make every service select by credentialId.

Team destination calendars dropped when organizer destination is null

`evt.destinationCalendar` is set to null when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. The following `if (COLLECTIVE) evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` silently does nothing in that case, so destination calendars collected from other hosts are discarded. A collective event whose organizer has no destination calendar but whose other hosts do will not invite those hosts. Initialize the array before pushing.

Only first old calendar event deleted when merging bookings

The method now processes all calendar references for the new booking, but the `newBookingId` merge cleanup still calls `booking.references.find(...)` and deletes a single old calendar event. For collective bookings with multiple calendar references, the remaining hosts' old events are left on their calendars after reschedule/merge. Recurring collective cancellation still only uses booking owner credentials

In the recurring/allRemainingBookings branch, the code still iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` and picks the first calendar reference from each updated booking, rather than using the current reference's credentialId/externalCalendarId. For collective recurring bookings, calendar events belonging to other hosts are not deleted. The new outer loop over bookingCalendarReference also re-runs this same deletion for every reference, causing duplicate delete attempts. Use the current reference to delete the matching event for each updated booking.

updateLocation references lose calendar external id and credential id

referencesToCreate in updateLocation now reads `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but CalendarManager.updateEvent's returned EventResult never populates either field. For calendar update results these values are undefined, so editLocation creates booking references without externalCalendarId/credentialId; later updates or cancellations must fall back to primary/all credentials. The old code used evt.destinationCalendar for these values. Either populate them in CalendarManager.updateEvent or keep the destination fallback.

Reschedule mutation returns before calendar/video deletion completes

After this PR getCalendar is awaited inside the callback, so the mutation can finish and sendRequestRescheduleEmail can send before any calendar or video deletion is initiated. Any rejection from getCalendar or deleteEvent is also unhandled. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` or a `for...of` loop.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. forEach is used with async callbacks, so the calendar/video deletion promises are never awaited. This causes fire-and-forget execution and unhandled rejections. Both recommend Promise.all with map or a for...of loop.

false_positives.candidate:
Recurring booking calendar deletes are pushed after Promise.all may have run

In the recurring-cancellation branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` is not awaited. The callbacks only push into apiDeletes after they resume from the awaited getCalendar/deleteEvent calls, so the later `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` can run with an empty or partial array. Calendar deletions for recurring bookings can therefore be skipped/unawaited and failures become unhandled rejections. Use a `for...of` loop with await or `await Promise.all(...map(...))`.
